title: The Path of the Law
license: Public domain (published 1897; JSTOR lists the issue as public domain). Free full text is also available from Project Gutenberg.

verified.evidence: Title, author, Harvard Law Review volume 10, issue 8, pages 457–478 and year 1897 matched on jstor.org (stable 1322028) and scilit.net (DOI 10.2307/1322028). Public-domain full text listed on gutenberg.org. Search results also note it was first delivered as an address at Boston University School of Law in January 1897 and printed in the Boston Law School Magazine shortly before the Harvard Law Review.

summary: An address on what lawyers actually study when they study law. Holmes argues that, for practical purposes, law is a set of predictions about what courts will do, and that viewing law through the eyes of a "bad man" who cares only about consequences helps separate legal rules from moral judgments. He criticizes the idea that legal development follows from logic alone and urges attention to history, policy and economics.
arguments: Law, for the practitioner, is a prediction of how courts will apply public force.
The "bad man" perspective separates what the law requires from what morality requires.
Legal reasoning dressed as logic often conceals judgments about social advantage that should be made explicit.
Lawyers should study the reasons and consequences of rules, not only their history.
strengths: Short, influential and freely available; gives non-lawyers a practical frame (law as forecast) that maps directly onto risk-based decision-making.
limitations: A nineteenth-century jurisprudential essay, not empirical work. The prediction theory has been criticized by later legal philosophers for neglecting why officials and citizens treat rules as obligations; some passages reflect the views and language of its time.
contested: The prediction theory is debated within jurisprudence; this course uses it as a working tool, not as a settled account of what law is.
generalizability: The frame transfers well to any organization that must estimate legal risk; it is a lens for thinking, not a method that produces numbers.
relevance: Teaches the executive habit of asking counsel for forecasts with conditions and confidence rather than verdicts.

title: Rules Versus Standards: An Economic Analysis
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced. A free copy is posted in the Duke Law Scholarship Repository and in Harvard's DASH repository.

verified.evidence: Title, author, Duke Law Journal volume 42, issue 3, pages 557–629, year 1992 and DOI 10.2307/1372840 matched on scholarship.law.duke.edu, hls.harvard.edu and dash.harvard.edu.

summary: An economic analysis of whether laws should take the form of rules, whose content is fixed before people act, or standards, whose content is supplied afterward by an adjudicator. Kaplow argues that rules cost more to promulgate and standards cost more to apply and to advise on, so the frequency of the regulated conduct is central to the choice. He separates the rule–standard question from the question of how detailed a law should be.
arguments: Rules are costlier to create; standards are costlier for individuals to interpret and for adjudicators to apply.
When conduct is frequent and similar, the up-front cost of a rule is spread across many cases, favoring rules.
People can learn rules cheaply before acting, so behavior tends to track rules more closely than standards.
The choice between rules and standards is distinct from the choice of how complex or detailed a law should be.
design: Formal economic analysis of legal form; no empirical data.
strengths: Clear, general framework that applies to statutes, contracts and internal policies; widely cited as the standard economic treatment.
limitations: A theoretical model; real legal systems mix rules and standards, and the costs it identifies are rarely measured. Long and technical in places.
generalizability: Transfers directly to organizational policy design (codes of conduct, approval thresholds, travel and compensation policies) and to contract drafting.
relevance: Gives the learner a principled way to decide when to write precise rules and when to rely on judgment, in contracts and in management systems.

title: Non-Contractual Relations in Business: A Preliminary Study
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Title, author, American Sociological Review volume 28, issue 1 (February 1963), pages 55–67 and JSTOR stable 2090458 matched in search results (JSTOR-derived PDF hosted at edisciplinas.usp.br; University of Wisconsin Law repository record; a Springer reprint in Stewart Macaulay: Selected Works). A journal DOI was not confirmed, so none is given.

summary: An exploratory interview study of how businesspeople actually manage exchange relationships. Macaulay reports that they often plan transactions incompletely and seldom use legal sanctions to adjust relationships or settle disputes, relying instead on reputation, continuing relationships and shared norms. The paper became a foundation of the "relational contract" and law-and-society traditions.
arguments: Businesspeople frequently leave exchanges only partly planned.
Legal sanctions are seldom used to adjust relationships or resolve disputes.
Non-legal sanctions — reputation, repeat dealing, personal relationships — do much of the enforcement work.
Formal contract planning has costs as well as benefits and is used selectively.
design: Exploratory interview study; the article reports interviews with 68 businesspeople.
strengths: Rich, grounded observation that challenged a purely doctrinal view of contracts; still a standard reading in contracts and economic sociology.
limitations: Interviews rather than measured outcomes; a particular time, region and industry mix; described by its author as preliminary.
contested: Later commentators accept the core observation but argue it needs specification: formal contracts may matter little in healthy ongoing relationships and much more at their end or in one-off deals. Contrast the doctrinal view summarized in R-ali-1981-restatement.
generalizability: Likely to generalize to repeat-dealing relationships in many industries, including sports; weaker for one-off, high-stakes or adversarial transactions.
relevance: Connects the learner's sociology background to contract practice: contracts work alongside relationships and reputation, and matter most when those fail.

title: Restatement of the Law Second, Contracts
publication: American Law Institute (reporters: Robert Braucher, to 1971; E. Allan Farnsworth, from 1971)
license: © The American Law Institute. Linked, not reproduced. Available in law libraries and legal research services.

verified.evidence: Title, publisher (American Law Institute), 1981 edition and reporters (Robert Braucher until 1971; E. Allan Farnsworth from 1971) matched on ali.org; the 1981 imprint is corroborated by Berkeley Law and Villanova Law library catalog records.

summary: The American Law Institute's synthesis of the U.S. common law of contracts, stated as black-letter rules with comments and illustrations. It covers formation, consideration and its substitutes, interpretation, conditions, performance and breach, and remedies. Courts frequently cite and adopt its sections, but it is a secondary authority that binds no court unless adopted.
arguments: Contract formation rests on mutual assent (offer and acceptance) and bargained-for consideration.
Some promises are enforceable without consideration because of reasonable reliance.
Interpretation seeks the parties' meaning in context, with tie-breaking principles for ambiguity.
Remedies protect the expectation, reliance or restitution interest, subject to limits such as foreseeability and mitigation.
design: Secondary legal authority: rules, comments and illustrations drafted by reporters and approved by the Institute, synthesizing U.S. case law.
strengths: The most widely cited single summary of mainstream U.S. contract doctrine; carefully organized and drafted.
limitations: Not binding; states depart from it on important points; it is from 1981 and does not govern sales of goods, which fall mainly under the Uniform Commercial Code. Expensive to access outside a library.
contested: Its doctrinal picture assumes formal contracts anchor commercial expectations; R-macaulay-1963-non-contractual documents how often businesspeople operate outside formal law.
generalizability: U.S.-specific; civil-law systems (including most of Latin America) organize contract law differently.
relevance: The reference point lawyers use when they describe "the general rule" in contracts; knowing what it is helps the learner ask whether a jurisdiction follows it.

title: Business Law I Essentials

verified.evidence: Title, publisher (OpenStax, Rice University), 2019 first-edition publication date (details page: September 27, 2019) and the CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 license matched on openstax.org (preface, details page and web PDF). Mirande Valbrune and Renee De Assis are listed first among the contributors; Suzanne Cardell, Tess C. Taylor and Natalie Sappleton are also listed. A second edition (2e) is listed on openstax.org with a June 24, 2026 publication date. summary: A free, openly licensed introductory business law textbook covering the U.S. legal system, contracts, torts, agency, employment, intellectual property, business organizations and related topics at an undergraduate level. It is designed for readers without legal training and includes examples and review questions.
arguments: Business law sits within a layered system of constitutional, statutory, regulatory and judge-made law.
Contracts require mutual assent, consideration, capacity and legality, with remedies for breach.
Agency and employment relationships create duties and liabilities for organizations.
Intellectual property law gives organizations distinct tools — copyright, patent, trademark and trade secret.
strengths: Free, accessible and openly licensed; good foundation for readers new to law.
limitations: Introductory and general; does not track recent state-law changes (for example on non-competes) and is not a substitute for current, jurisdiction-specific advice. The license is non-commercial, not CC BY.
generalizability: U.S.-centric general principles; useful as vocabulary for any U.S. organization.
relevance: The week's open foundation text: the learner can fill gaps in legal vocabulary without paywalls.

title: Noncompete Agreements in the US Labor Force
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced. A free copy is posted in the University of Michigan Law School repository; an earlier version is on SSRN (abstract 2625714).

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Journal of Law and Economics volume 64, issue 1, pages 53–84, year 2021 and DOI 10.1086/712206 matched on econpapers.repec.org, chicagounbound.uchicago.edu and repository.law.umich.edu. Survey size and headline findings matched the published abstract.

summary: Uses a nationally representative survey of 11,505 U.S. labor force participants to describe who signs non-competes, when and on what terms. About 18 percent were bound at the time of the survey and 38 percent had agreed to one at some point. Non-competes appear in low-wage as well as high-wage jobs and in states that do not enforce them; few workers negotiate, and many learn of the clause after accepting an offer.
arguments: Roughly 18 percent of labor force participants were bound by a non-compete; 38 percent had signed one at some point.
Non-competes are more common in high-skill, high-pay jobs but also appear in low-wage jobs and in non-enforcing states.
Only about 10 percent of workers report negotiating over the non-compete; about one-third are presented with it after accepting the offer.
Workers told early about a non-compete fare better than those told late; wages are relatively lower where non-competes are easier to enforce.
design: Nationally representative cross-sectional survey of 11,505 labor force participants, with comparisons across state enforceability regimes.
strengths: The first large representative evidence on non-compete prevalence and process; published in a leading law-and-economics journal.
limitations: Self-reported survey data; associations between enforceability and outcomes are observational and could reflect other state differences. An earlier working-paper version reported different prevalence figures, so cite the published article.
contested: Whether non-competes mainly protect investment (training, trade secrets) or mainly suppress mobility and wages remains debated; see the quasi-experimental evidence in R-marx-2009-mobility.
generalizability: Describes the U.S. labor force broadly; sector-specific patterns (including sports organizations) are not separately reported.
relevance: Grounds the restrictive-covenant lesson in data and shows how often a "standard" clause is imposed rather than negotiated.

title: Mobility, Skills, and the Michigan Non-Compete Experiment
license: Copyright holder's terms. Linked, not reproduced. An author/working-paper version is hosted by the Fung Institute at UC Berkeley.

verified.evidence: Title, authors, Management Science volume 55, issue 6 (June 2009), pages 875–889 and DOI 10.1287/mnsc.1080.0985 matched on pubsonline.informs.org and econpapers.repec.org; design and headline estimates matched the Berkeley-hosted paper.

summary: Treats Michigan's 1985 reversal of its policy of not enforcing non-competes as a natural experiment. Comparing inventors in Michigan with inventors in states that continued not to enforce, the authors estimate that mobility fell after the reversal, with larger effects for inventors with firm-specific skills and for specialists.
arguments: Enforcing non-competes reduced inventor mobility in Michigan by about 8.1 percent relative to comparison states.
The effect was larger for inventors with more firm-specific skills (about 15.4 percent at one standard deviation above the mean).
The effect was larger for specialists in narrow technical fields (about 16.2 percent at one standard deviation above the mean).
design: Difference-in-differences around Michigan's 1985 policy reversal, comparing inventors in Michigan with inventors in states that continued not to enforce non-competes.
strengths: A credible natural-experiment design that addresses the selection problems of cross-sectional comparisons.
limitations: One state, one period and one occupational group (inventors); measures mobility, not wages or welfare; relies on the comparison states being a valid counterfactual.
contested: Consistent with harm-to-mobility arguments; defenders of non-competes argue that reduced mobility can protect training and information investments. See R-starr-2021-noncompete.
generalizability: Strongest for technical knowledge workers; transfer to other occupations, including coaching and analytics roles, is plausible but untested here.
relevance: Shows how to read causal evidence on a legal rule — and what it cannot tell an executive.

title: Non-Compete Clause Rule
publication: Federal Register, 89 FR 38342–38506 (final rule published May 7, 2024; 16 CFR Parts 910 and 912)
license: Official U.S. government publication. Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Rule title, Federal Register citation 89 FR 38342 (document 2024-09171, pages 38342–38506), May 7, 2024 publication and the scheduled September 4, 2024 effective date matched in gao.gov (B-336417) and Federal Register mirrors. Status: the August 20, 2024 set-aside in Ryan LLC v. FTC (N.D. Tex., Judge Ada Brown) matched in multiple law-firm reports; the FTC's 3–1 vote on September 5, 2025 to dismiss its appeals and accede to vacatur matched on ftc.gov (the linked press release). Removal of the rule from the Code of Federal Regulations by Federal Register document 2026-02866 (91 FR 6507, published February 12, 2026) appeared on an ftc.gov public-comments page and Federal Register mirrors, not on federalregister.gov itself, so that detail is partially confirmed. The URL points to the FTC's September 2025 announcement because the rule's own Federal Register page was not seen in search results.

summary: The FTC's 2024 final rule treated most worker non-competes as an unfair method of competition under Section 5 of the FTC Act and, with exceptions, would have barred employers from entering into or enforcing them, while allowing existing non-competes with senior executives to remain in force. A federal district court set the rule aside on August 20, 2024, before its September 4, 2024 effective date; on September 5, 2025 the Commission voted 3–1 to dismiss its appeals and accede to vacatur, and in February 2026 the rule's text was removed from the Code of Federal Regulations. The FTC has said it will pursue non-competes case by case under Section 5; state law continues to govern enforceability.
arguments: The FTC framed non-competes as an unfair method of competition harmful to workers and competition.
The district court held that the FTC lacked statutory authority to issue the rule and that the rule was arbitrary and capricious, and gave its order nationwide effect.
After abandoning the rule, the FTC said it would rely on individual enforcement actions rather than a categorical ban.
design: Federal agency final rule and its subsequent litigation history.
strengths: Primary source for the federal policy debate; the rulemaking record collected extensive argument and evidence on non-competes.
limitations: The rule never took effect; its record reflects the agency's position, and the court that set it aside ruled on authority and process, not on the economic merits. Status details after September 2025 come partly from secondary reports.
contested: The economic case against non-competes in the rulemaking is contested by those who argue non-competes protect investment; see R-starr-2021-noncompete and R-marx-2009-mobility for the evidence.
generalizability: U.S. federal context only; actual enforceability depends on state law and, outside the U.S., on national law.
relevance: A current, concrete example of how legal rules change, get challenged and depend on institutional authority — essential context before relying on anything said about non-competes.

title: Smith v. Van Gorkom, 488 A.2d 858
license: Judicial opinion (public record). Linked via Justia, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Case name, citation 488 A.2d 858, court (Supreme Court of Delaware) and 1985 decision matched on law.justia.com and opencasebook.org; the holding (directors who approved a merger without informing themselves were grossly negligent, breached the duty of care and lost business-judgment-rule protection) matched in several case summaries. Some summaries give a January 29, 1985 decision date.

summary: The Delaware Supreme Court held that the directors of a public company breached their duty of care by approving a cash-out merger without first informing themselves of reasonably available information, and that their decision was therefore not protected by the business judgment rule. The court reversed the lower court's judgment for the directors and sent the case back for a determination of damages.
arguments: The business judgment rule presumes an informed decision; it does not protect directors who failed to inform themselves.
The duty to make an informed decision is a duty of care, breached by gross negligence in the process.
A favorable price does not by itself cure an uninformed decision process.
design: Appellate judicial decision reviewing a board's approval of a merger.
strengths: Canonical case on the duty of care; widely taught; illustrates process-based review clearly.
limitations: One state's law (Delaware) and one fact pattern; later legal developments changed how often directors face personal liability for care claims; summaries simplify a long opinion.
contested: The decision has long been debated: some see it as a needed demand for diligence, others as encouraging defensive documentation.
generalizability: Delaware law governs many U.S. corporations, so the principles are influential; nonprofits, public bodies and non-U.S. entities follow different rules.
relevance: Teaches that leaders are judged on the quality of their decision process — a principle that applies inside any organization.

title: Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383
authors: Supreme Court of the United States
license: Official U.S. government publication (United States Reports). Linked, not reproduced.

verified.evidence: Case name, citation 449 U.S. 383 (1981), decision date January 13, 1981 and majority opinion by Justice Rehnquist matched on govinfo.gov, law.cornell.edu and americanbar.org; holdings (rejection of the "control group" test; work-product doctrine applies to IRS summonses) matched in the official syllabus.

summary: The Supreme Court held that the attorney-client privilege can protect communications between a corporation's counsel and employees below senior management, made to gather information needed to give the corporation legal advice. The case arose from an internal investigation into questionable foreign payments, in which counsel used questionnaires and interviews; the IRS sought those materials. The Court also held that the work-product doctrine applies to IRS summonses.
arguments: A narrow "control group" test would discourage the flow of information counsel needs and is rejected.
Communications from employees to corporate counsel, made at the direction of superiors to secure legal advice, can be privileged.
The privilege protects communications, not the underlying facts.
Work-product protection applies to materials prepared in anticipation of litigation, including in tax-summons proceedings.
strengths: The foundational federal case on corporate privilege; short and readable.
limitations: Applies to federal law; state privilege rules and other countries' rules can differ, and later cases refine how privilege applies to in-house counsel and mixed business-legal communications.
generalizability: Applies to U.S. organizations of all kinds in federal matters; the practical habits it implies transfer widely.
relevance: Explains why organizational lawyers say "I represent the company" and why forwarding legal advice can waive protection.
